**Rate split deepens on the RBA board**

The Reserve Bank board is more divided than its last decision let on, and the split is shifting bets towards a long pause.

Minutes of the Melbourne Cup Day meeting, published yesterday, show the six-to-three vote to take the cash rate to 4.85 per cent was closer in substance than in numbers. The three members who voted against the rise argued another increase risked tipping the economy into a sharp downturn.

Their case rested on three things: unemployment has already risen to 4.7 per cent, quicker than the bank forecast; growth is slowing; and house prices are still falling. They also noted earlier rises have not yet fully passed through to households.

The governor has not moved. In a speech yesterday she said some firms now treat inflation of three to three-and-a-half per cent as normal, well above the 2.5 per cent the bank aims for.

**Treasurer flags simpler tax rules**

The Treasurer outlined plans to simplify tax rules for sole traders and employers, which he said could save businesses more than $50 million a year in compliance costs, and promised spending cuts in next month's budget update.

**Department store collapse leaves large debts**

A collapsed department store chain owes more than $180 million to lenders and suppliers, and customers are holding about $33 million in unused gift cards.

## Sentiment watch

**Buyers turn gloomy on house prices**

A monthly housing sentiment survey shows expectations for house prices fell 13.4% to 99.6 in November, the first reading below 100 since late 2022. Respondents are now evenly split between those expecting falls and those expecting rises.
